Q: what does the acrosome do in a sperm cell
A: "The acrosome is an organelle that develops over the anterior half of the head of sperm cells. It contains digestive enzymes, such as hyaluronidase and acrosin, which are crucial for penetrating the outer membrane of the ovum, known as the zona pellucida. During fertilization, the acrosome undergoes a reaction (the acrosome reaction) that allows the sperm to release these enzymes, facilitating its ability to penetrate the egg and ultimately join with the egg's nucleus. This process is essential for successful fertilization."

single_nq_dev_2764
the kinked demand curve in oligopoly is used to explain
A: ["Kinked demand", "Kinked demand", "Kinked demand", "Oligopoly", "Oligopoly", "Kinked demand", "Oligopoly", "Kinked demand"]
Q: the kinked demand curve in oligopoly is used to explain
A: "The kinked demand curve in oligopoly is used to explain sticky prices and the behavior of firms in an oligopolistic market. It suggests that prices remain stable despite changes in marginal costs due to the interdependence of firms; if one firm raises its prices, others may not follow, leading to a loss of market share for the firm that increased prices. Conversely, if a firm lowers its prices, others will likely follow to maintain their market share, resulting in a kink in the demand curve. This model illustrates why prices in oligopolistic markets can be rigid and do not adjust easily to changes in demand or cost."
A: The kinked demand curve in oligopoly is used to explain sticky prices and the behavior of firms in an oligopolistic market. It suggests that prices remain stable despite changes in marginal costs due to the interdependence of firms; if one firm raises its prices, others may not follow, leading to a loss of market share for the firm that increased prices. Conversely, if a firm lowers its prices, others will likely follow to maintain their market share, resulting in a kink in the demand curve. This model illustrates why prices in oligopolistic markets can be rigid and do not adjust easily to changes in demand or cost

why do longer dna molecules move more slowly than shorter ones during electrophoresis
A: ["Gel electrophoresis", "Agarose gel electrophoresis", "Agarose gel electrophoresis", "Agarose gel electrophoresis", "Agarose gel electrophoresis", "Gel electrophoresis of nucleic acids", "Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis", "Gel electrophoresis of nucleic acids"]
Q: why do longer dna molecules move more slowly than shorter ones during electrophoresis
A: "Longer DNA molecules move more slowly than shorter ones during electrophoresis because they encounter more resistance as they navigate through the gel matrix. The gel acts as a sieving medium, with pores that impede the movement of larger molecules. Shorter DNA fragments can pass through these pores more easily and quickly, while longer fragments are hindered by their size, resulting in slower migration through the gel. This phenomenon is known as sieving, where the size of the DNA molecules affects their ability to move through the gel."
A: Longer DNA molecules move more slowly than shorter ones during electrophoresis because they encounter more resistance as they navigate through the gel matrix. Shorter DNA fragments can pass through these pores more easily and quickly, while longer fragments are hindered by their size, resulting in slower migration through the gel. This phenomenon is known as sieving, where the size of the DNA molecules affects their ability to move through the gel
